findings.text: The first sentence tells a newcomer clearly what Athena is. That answers "what is this" right away.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository."

findings.text: None of these features appear on the rest of the page. There is no request, no second-model check and no cost record, so the newcomer has to take Athena's main selling points on trust while the page shows something else: a study of another project.
findings.source: "It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: This is Athena's home URL, but almost all of the page explains firstmate, a different tool. The lede says why, but a newcomer who came to learn about Athena gets only three sentences about it before a long, technical description of firstmate.
findings.source: <h1> "Athena explains how firstmate handles work" and the lede "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project..."

findings.text: Next steps are linked from the top and listed at the end, which is good. But "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" gives no clone command and no prerequisites, such as a Rust toolchain or model API keys. So `athena ask "add a changelog"` may not work for someone following only this page.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself" (header) and the "Next steps" section

findings.text: Firstmate is explained in plain words early on, and the "Words used first" list defines terms before they are used. A newcomer can say what firstmate does after the Start here section.
findings.source: "Firstmate is a tool that keeps a backlog of programming tasks and hands each one to a separate AI coding tool, called a worker..." (Start here)

findings.text: The definitions are honest but repetitive. yolo, green, red and in scope appear in Words used first, in the body text and again in the Glossary, which makes an already dense page longer.
findings.source: "in scope" definition: "The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope, so this page gives no test for it."; yolo, green and red are each defined three times

findings.text: Internal ids are used before or without explanation. The t-numbers appear before the Transitions section, the ra ids are never explained, and the reader is not told why exit status 75 matters. A newcomer will find these opaque.
findings.source: Counters: "places-held, changed by transitions t1, t3, t4, t9, t11"; "ra1"…"ra6"; "exit 75"

findings.text: Every statement is cited, and every claim links to the exact lines at a pinned commit. This shows convincingly why Athena might matter: its explanations can be checked.
findings.source: "Each statement below ends with the id of the claim that supports it"; the "Claims and sources" section with line-level GitHub links

findings.text: Some text is about the study's own production process, which a newcomer does not need. It also refers to a studies/ folder that the page never links to.
findings.source: About this page: "the name of the folder under studies/ that holds the data this page is generated from"; Limits f3: "A first reading of the pinned tree missed these paths"
